title: Inflammation II — Chronic Inflammation & Disease
source: Inflammation LS5009  lectures 1 and 2 student copy.pdf

cards.explanation: These processes occur simultaneously rather than as three entirely separate chronological stages.
cards.text: Chronic inflammation combines ongoing inflammation, tissue destruction and {{c1::attempted repair}}.
cards.question: Chronic inflammation combines ongoing inflammation, tissue destruction and {{c1::attempted repair}}.

cards.explanation: The lecture names macrophages, lymphocytes and plasma cells.
cards.text: The typical chronic infiltrate is predominantly {{c1::mononuclear cells}}.
cards.question: The typical chronic infiltrate is predominantly {{c1::mononuclear cells}}.

cards.explanation: Both may coexist with active injury, rather than establishing that the inflammatory process has ended.
cards.text: Repair during chronic inflammation can cause fibrosis and {{c1::angiogenesis}}.
cards.question: Repair during chronic inflammation can cause fibrosis and {{c1::angiogenesis}}.

cards.explanation: Tuberculosis is a named example; chronic responses may begin primarily or follow unresolved/recurrent acute inflammation.
cards.text: An infection that is not eradicated can sustain {{c1::chronic inflammation}}.
cards.question: An infection that is not eradicated can sustain {{c1::chronic inflammation}}.

cards.explanation: The source uses pulmonary silicosis as an example of persistent exogenous material.
cards.text: Prolonged silica exposure can sustain chronic inflammation in the {{c1::lung}}.
cards.question: Prolonged silica exposure can sustain chronic inflammation in the {{c1::lung}}.

cards.explanation: The stimulus need not be a new external infection.
cards.text: An immune response against self antigens can perpetuate {{c1::autoimmune inflammation}}.
cards.question: An immune response against self antigens can perpetuate {{c1::autoimmune inflammation}}.

cards.explanation: Whether inflammation occurs depends on material and host context; implantation does not mean every prosthesis causes a granuloma.
cards.text: Sutures, asbestos fibres and implanted material can act as persistent {{c1::foreign-body stimuli}}.
cards.question: Sutures, asbestos fibres and implanted material can act as persistent {{c1::foreign-body stimuli}}.

cards.explanation: The source labels chronic inflammation “adaptive”; this is too exclusive, because innate macrophages and other cells remain central.
cards.text: A continuing stimulus can produce a repetitive cycle of recruitment, injury and {{c1::repair}}.
cards.question: A continuing stimulus can produce a repetitive cycle of recruitment, injury and {{c1::repair}}.

cards.explanation: Both increased collagen synthesis and reduced breakdown can contribute.
cards.text: Fibrosis develops when matrix production exceeds matrix {{c1::degradation}}.
cards.question: Fibrosis develops when matrix production exceeds matrix {{c1::degradation}}.

cards.explanation: The source pathway connects this with extracellular-matrix accumulation.
cards.text: Reduced matrix metalloproteinase activity can decrease {{c1::collagen degradation}}.
cards.question: Reduced matrix metalloproteinase activity can decrease {{c1::collagen degradation}}.

cards.explanation: Their growth factors and cytokines link persistent inflammation with scar production.
cards.text: Activated macrophages and lymphocytes can stimulate {{c1::fibroblast proliferation}}.
cards.question: Activated macrophages and lymphocytes can stimulate {{c1::fibroblast proliferation}}.

cards.explanation: FGF and PDGF also appear in the diagram; the response depends on cell type and context.
cards.text: A major fibrogenic growth factor in the source pathway is {{c1::TGF-β}}.
cards.question: A major fibrogenic growth factor in the source pathway is {{c1::TGF-β}}.

cards.explanation: This is one illustrated pathway; tissue macrophage populations also have developmental origins not fully represented by this older schematic.
cards.text: The circulating leukocyte that can enter tissue and become a macrophage is the {{c1::monocyte}}.
cards.question: The circulating leukocyte that can enter tissue and become a macrophage is the {{c1::monocyte}}.

cards.explanation: The diagram also includes non-immune triggers such as microbial products; activation is not exclusively antibody mediated.
cards.text: The T-cell cytokine highlighted for macrophage activation is {{c1::IFN-γ}}.
cards.question: The T-cell cytokine highlighted for macrophage activation is {{c1::IFN-γ}}.

cards.explanation: Their antimicrobial products can also damage surrounding host tissue.
cards.text: Activated macrophages can sustain injury through proteases and {{c1::reactive oxygen metabolites}}.
cards.question: Activated macrophages can sustain injury through proteases and {{c1::reactive oxygen metabolites}}.

cards.explanation: The source links PDGF, FGF and TGF-β with fibrogenic responses. A repair signal is not necessarily beneficial if prolonged.
cards.text: Macrophage-derived growth factors can drive {{c1::fibrosis}} as well as repair.
cards.question: Macrophage-derived growth factors can drive {{c1::fibrosis}} as well as repair.

cards.explanation: This describes a pattern, not absence of a cause or lack of clinical importance.
cards.text: Diffuse accumulation of macrophages and lymphocytes without organised granulomas is {{c1::non-specific chronic inflammation}}.
cards.question: Diffuse accumulation of macrophages and lymphocytes without organised granulomas is {{c1::non-specific chronic inflammation}}.

cards.explanation: Normal connective/parenchymal tissue can be replaced by scar, impairing organ structure and function.
cards.text: Chronic bowel-wall scarring may narrow the lumen and produce a {{c1::stricture}}.
cards.question: Chronic bowel-wall scarring may narrow the lumen and produce a {{c1::stricture}}.

cards.explanation: They often take an epithelioid appearance. A fixed size or minimum five-cell count is not a universal diagnostic definition.
cards.text: A granuloma is an organised aggregate of activated {{c1::macrophages}}.
cards.question: A granuloma is an organised aggregate of activated {{c1::macrophages}}.

cards.explanation: They remain macrophage-lineage cells; their appearance does not make them epithelial cells.
cards.text: Macrophages with an epithelial-like appearance are called {{c1::epithelioid histiocytes}}.
cards.question: Macrophages with an epithelial-like appearance are called {{c1::epithelioid histiocytes}}.

cards.explanation: Persistent microbes and foreign material can both be associated with this pattern.
cards.text: Granulomatous inflammation can help contain material that is difficult to {{c1::eradicate or digest}}.
cards.question: Granulomatous inflammation can help contain material that is difficult to {{c1::eradicate or digest}}.

cards.explanation: Correction to the source list: placing sarcoidosis among microorganisms causing disease is misleading; granulomatous morphology is not synonymous with infection.
cards.text: Sarcoidosis is a granulomatous condition, but is {{c1::not an established infection by a named microorganism}}.
cards.question: Sarcoidosis is a granulomatous condition, but is {{c1::not an established infection by a named microorganism}}.
cards.answer: not an established infection by a named microorganism

cards.explanation: A granuloma is an organised macrophage-rich inflammatory structure; granulation tissue is vessel/fibroblast-rich repair tissue.
cards.text: Granulomatous inflammation and granulation tissue are {{c1::different processes}}.
cards.question: Granulomatous inflammation and granulation tissue are {{c1::different processes}}.

cards.explanation: The figure distinguishes fusion from transformation into a single epithelioid macrophage.
cards.text: Fusion of macrophages can produce {{c1::multinucleated giant cells}}.
cards.question: Fusion of macrophages can produce {{c1::multinucleated giant cells}}.

cards.explanation: Occasional plasma cells may also occur; exact architecture varies with cause and stage.
cards.text: A granuloma commonly includes a surrounding component of {{c1::lymphocytes}}.
cards.question: A granuloma commonly includes a surrounding component of {{c1::lymphocytes}}.

cards.explanation: The source histology is attributed to a minipig model; it is not labelled as a human patient sample.
cards.text: The TB example shows a necrotic centre surrounded by an organised {{c1::granulomatous response}}.
cards.question: The TB example shows a necrotic centre surrounded by an organised {{c1::granulomatous response}}.

cards.explanation: Vasodilation contributes, whereas systemic fever involves regulated thermoregulatory signalling.
cards.text: Local redness and heat mainly reflect {{c1::increased local blood flow}}.
cards.question: Local redness and heat mainly reflect {{c1::increased local blood flow}}.

cards.explanation: These include acute-phase protein changes, leukocyte changes and constitutional symptoms.
cards.text: Inflammatory mediators entering the circulation can produce {{c1::systemic manifestations}}.
cards.question: Inflammatory mediators entering the circulation can produce {{c1::systemic manifestations}}.

cards.explanation: CRP is a named example; a raised marker is not specific for one disease.
cards.text: The plasma proteins whose concentrations change during inflammation are {{c1::acute-phase reactants}}.
cards.question: The plasma proteins whose concentrations change during inflammation are {{c1::acute-phase reactants}}.

cards.explanation: It is a possible systemic response, not something present in every severe infection.
cards.text: An increased circulating white-cell count is {{c1::leukocytosis}}.
cards.question: An increased circulating white-cell count is {{c1::leukocytosis}}.

cards.explanation: The lecture lists lymph-node enlargement with fever and blood changes; enlargement alone does not identify a cause.
cards.text: Enlarged draining lymph nodes are a possible {{c1::systemic or regional inflammatory manifestation}}.
cards.question: Enlarged draining lymph nodes are a possible {{c1::systemic or regional inflammatory manifestation}}.

cards.explanation: This clarifies the lecture’s list of severe systemic responses: sepsis is not simply any inflammation, fever or circulating cytokine increase.
cards.text: Sepsis involves life-threatening organ dysfunction from a dysregulated response to {{c1::infection}}.
cards.question: Sepsis involves life-threatening organ dysfunction from a dysregulated response to {{c1::infection}}.

cards.explanation: The source names it but gives no complete diagnostic criteria or treatment algorithm; neither is invented here.
cards.text: Septic shock is a severe sepsis-related {{c1::circulatory and metabolic dysfunction}} state.
cards.question: Septic shock is a severe sepsis-related {{c1::circulatory and metabolic dysfunction}} state.

cards.explanation: They promote fever signalling, including effects on hypothalamic thermoregulation.
cards.text: IL-1, IL-6 and TNF can act as endogenous {{c1::pyrogens}}.
cards.question: IL-1, IL-6 and TNF can act as endogenous {{c1::pyrogens}}.

cards.explanation: The cytokines subsequently released by host cells are endogenous mediators; these are different sources.
cards.text: Microbial products triggering host pyrogen release are called {{c1::exogenous pyrogens}}.
cards.question: Microbial products triggering host pyrogen release are called {{c1::exogenous pyrogens}}.

cards.explanation: This differentiates regulated fever from simply warming a locally inflamed area. The lecture’s claim that most pathogens prefer temperatures below 37°C is overgeneralised.
cards.text: Fever reflects an increased hypothalamic temperature {{c1::set point}}.
cards.question: Fever reflects an increased hypothalamic temperature {{c1::set point}}.

cards.explanation: This is a possible benefit, not a claim that every fever is harmless or that all pathogens stop growing above body temperature.
cards.text: Raised temperature can enhance some immune functions, including {{c1::antigen processing}}.
cards.question: Raised temperature can enhance some immune functions, including {{c1::antigen processing}}.

cards.explanation: The lecture connects this metabolic change with type 2 diabetes risk; it is not the sole mechanism or a diagnostic rule.
cards.text: Persistent inflammatory signalling can impair {{c1::insulin signalling}}.
cards.question: Persistent inflammatory signalling can impair {{c1::insulin signalling}}.

cards.explanation: This is a contributory mechanism, not proof that every chronic inflammatory condition causes cancer.
cards.text: Chronic inflammation can support tumour initiation, growth and {{c1::metastatic progression}}.
cards.question: Chronic inflammation can support tumour initiation, growth and {{c1::metastatic progression}}.

cards.explanation: New blood vessels support growing tissue; the presence of angiogenesis does not by itself mean malignancy.
cards.text: A process shared by wound repair and tumour growth is {{c1::angiogenesis}}.
cards.question: A process shared by wound repair and tumour growth is {{c1::angiogenesis}}.

cards.explanation: Changes in matrix and cell attachment influence migration, but the biological control of the two settings differs.
cards.text: Repair and tumour progression can both involve remodelling of the {{c1::extracellular matrix}}.
cards.question: Repair and tumour progression can both involve remodelling of the {{c1::extracellular matrix}}.

cards.explanation: It highlights persistent repair-like signalling and histological parallels, not that normal wound healing is itself cancer.
cards.text: The phrase “tumours are wounds that do not heal” is a {{c1::biological analogy}}.
cards.question: The phrase “tumours are wounds that do not heal” is a {{c1::biological analogy}}.

cards.explanation: The source discusses overlapping gene programmes without establishing identical regulation or inevitable transformation.
cards.text: Growth factors and cytokines can support cell survival, proliferation and {{c1::migration}} in both repair and tumours.
cards.question: Growth factors and cytokines can support cell survival, proliferation and {{c1::migration}} in both repair and tumours.

cards.explanation: This supplementary model investigates tissue repair. Cell counts, culture timing and fixative details are not turned into core exam filler.
cards.text: The organotypic skin model combines epithelial cells with a fibroblast-containing {{c1::collagen matrix}}.
cards.question: The organotypic skin model combines epithelial cells with a fibroblast-containing {{c1::collagen matrix}}.

cards.explanation: This allows comparison of epithelial closure over the model substrate. It is a conceptual description, not a protocol for reproducing the experiment.
cards.text: The illustrated wound model removes an area of epidermis while retaining the underlying {{c1::matrix}}.
cards.question: The illustrated wound model removes an area of epidermis while retaining the underlying {{c1::matrix}}.

cards.explanation: The images are labelled 0 h,24 h,4 d and7 d. No quantitative migration rate or clinical wound-healing timetable is inferred from them.
cards.text: Serial sections of the model compare repair at different {{c1::time points}}.
cards.question: Serial sections of the model compare repair at different {{c1::time points}}.

cards.explanation: The source places repair and tumour schematics together to compare shared signalling with different outcomes.
cards.text: Unlike controlled wound repair, invasive tumour growth can show {{c1::persistent dysregulated tissue invasion}}.
cards.question: Unlike controlled wound repair, invasive tumour growth can show {{c1::persistent dysregulated tissue invasion}}.

cards.explanation: The hallmarks overview is a comparison prompt; it does not establish that inflammation alone supplies every hallmark or causes every tumour.
cards.text: A tumour-associated inflammatory response can help sustain a permissive {{c1::microenvironment}}.
cards.question: A tumour-associated inflammatory response can help sustain a permissive {{c1::microenvironment}}.

cards.explanation: The source contrasts therapeutic/pathological inflammation. Effects depend on cell composition, signalling and timing rather than all inflammation being uniformly pro-cancer.
cards.text: Inflammation may have tumour-promoting or tumour-restraining effects depending on {{c1::context}}.
cards.question: Inflammation may have tumour-promoting or tumour-restraining effects depending on {{c1::context}}.

cards.explanation: The source’s “spouting” is a typographical error.
cards.text: Repair-associated angiogenesis commonly occurs by {{c1::sprouting from existing vessels}}.
cards.question: Repair-associated angiogenesis commonly occurs by {{c1::sprouting from existing vessels}}.

cards.explanation: The diagram associates its behaviour with VEGF and Notch signalling; it is not a separate immune-cell type.
cards.text: The leading endothelial cell in a vessel sprout is the {{c1::tip cell}}.
cards.question: The leading endothelial cell in a vessel sprout is the {{c1::tip cell}}.

cards.explanation: This permits endothelial migration; later stabilisation requires re-establishment of supporting structures.
cards.text: Matrix metalloproteinases assist sprouting by degrading the {{c1::basement membrane}}.
cards.question: Matrix metalloproteinases assist sprouting by degrading the {{c1::basement membrane}}.

cards.explanation: The source illustrates recruitment after sprout extension.
cards.text: Recruitment of {{c1::pericytes}} helps stabilise newly formed vessels.
cards.question: Recruitment of {{c1::pericytes}} helps stabilise newly formed vessels.

cards.explanation: The older diagram’s Th1/Th2 labels are simplified: IL-1 and TNF are not exclusive Th1 products, and cytokine effects are not a universal two-box classification.
cards.text: The balance of cytokines and chemokines helps determine the tumour {{c1::inflammatory infiltrate}}.
cards.question: The balance of cytokines and chemokines helps determine the tumour {{c1::inflammatory infiltrate}}.

cards.explanation: The source contrasts pro-angiogenic and angiostatic outcomes. It is an illustrative model, not a prediction from one cytokine measurement in a patient.
cards.text: Chemokine effects on vascularisation can alter {{c1::tumour growth}}.
cards.question: Chemokine effects on vascularisation can alter {{c1::tumour growth}}.

cards.explanation: This combines the three core chronic processes in one histological example.
cards.text: Chronic lung inflammation shows inflammatory cells, tissue destruction and {{c1::fibrosis}}.
cards.question: Chronic lung inflammation shows inflammatory cells, tissue destruction and {{c1::fibrosis}}.

cards.explanation: The source contrasts this with mononuclear inflammation, parenchymal loss and connective-tissue replacement in chronic disease.
cards.text: In acute bronchopneumonia, the dominant cells filling alveolar spaces are {{c1::neutrophils}}.
cards.question: In acute bronchopneumonia, the dominant cells filling alveolar spaces are {{c1::neutrophils}}.

cards.explanation: Its surrounding cellular architecture supports interpretation; central necrosis alone is not organism identification.
cards.text: The central zone in the illustrated tuberculous granuloma is {{c1::necrotic}}.
cards.question: The central zone in the illustrated tuberculous granuloma is {{c1::necrotic}}.

cards.explanation: Langhans-type giant cells are not Langerhans dendritic cells. Morphology alone is not uniquely specific for tuberculosis.
cards.text: The large multinucleated macrophage-derived cells labelled in the TB example are {{c1::Langhans-type giant cells}}.
cards.question: The large multinucleated macrophage-derived cells labelled in the TB example are {{c1::Langhans-type giant cells}}.

cards.explanation: These accompany epithelioid macrophages and giant cells rather than replacing them as the defining central cell type.
cards.text: The periphery of the illustrated granuloma contains a rim of {{c1::lymphocytes}}.
cards.question: The periphery of the illustrated granuloma contains a rim of {{c1::lymphocytes}}.

cards.explanation: The lecture identifies a role in myocardial infarction, stroke and ischaemic gangrene; these outcomes do not occur in every plaque.
cards.text: Atherosclerosis combines lipid accumulation with an {{c1::inflammatory response}}.
cards.question: Atherosclerosis combines lipid accumulation with an {{c1::inflammatory response}}.

cards.explanation: The source describes collections of dark-blue lymphocytes in chronically inflamed tissue.
cards.text: The rheumatoid arthritis histology example is taken from the joint {{c1::synovium}}.
cards.question: The rheumatoid arthritis histology example is taken from the joint {{c1::synovium}}.

cards.explanation: This contrasts with a local acute response to a transient traumatic insult.
cards.text: Rheumatoid arthritis illustrates chronic {{c1::autoimmune inflammation}}.
cards.question: Rheumatoid arthritis illustrates chronic {{c1::autoimmune inflammation}}.

cards.explanation: The source contrasts this distribution with the possible full gastrointestinal distribution of Crohn’s disease.
cards.text: Ulcerative colitis principally involves the mucosal lining of the rectum and {{c1::colon}}.
cards.question: Ulcerative colitis principally involves the mucosal lining of the rectum and {{c1::colon}}.

cards.explanation: This distribution does not mean every person has disease throughout the entire tract.
cards.text: Crohn’s disease may involve the gastrointestinal tract from mouth to {{c1::anus}}.
cards.question: Crohn’s disease may involve the gastrointestinal tract from mouth to {{c1::anus}}.

cards.explanation: The slide supplies a labelled histology example. Their absence does not exclude Crohn’s, and the appearance is not a stand-alone diagnosis.
cards.text: Granulomas can occur in {{c1::Crohn’s disease}}.
cards.question: Granulomas can occur in {{c1::Crohn’s disease}}.

cards.explanation: The source emphasises ulcerative colitis. Risk depends on factors such as extent and duration; no individual percentage or surveillance schedule is supplied.
cards.text: Long-standing colonic inflammatory disease can raise {{c1::colorectal cancer risk}}.
cards.question: Long-standing colonic inflammatory disease can raise {{c1::colorectal cancer risk}}.

cards.explanation: The lecture links tissue stress and immune-cell accumulation rather than treating fat as only passive storage.
cards.text: Visceral adipose tissue can recruit {{c1::macrophages}} during chronic metabolic inflammation.
cards.question: Visceral adipose tissue can recruit {{c1::macrophages}} during chronic metabolic inflammation.

cards.explanation: These markers are not uniquely diagnostic of obesity or one disease.
cards.text: The source names TNF, IL-6 and CRP as markers associated with {{c1::metabolic inflammation}}.
cards.question: The source names TNF, IL-6 and CRP as markers associated with {{c1::metabolic inflammation}}.

cards.explanation: It produces hormones/cytokines and interacts with liver, heart and muscle, not just an inert energy depot.
cards.text: Adipose tissue acts as an {{c1::endocrine and signalling organ}}.
cards.question: Adipose tissue acts as an {{c1::endocrine and signalling organ}}.

cards.explanation: This is a model of adipokine dysregulation, not a rule allowing clinical diagnosis from one hormone value.
cards.text: In the obesity-related schematic, adiponectin is shown {{c1::decreased}}.
cards.question: In the obesity-related schematic, adiponectin is shown {{c1::decreased}}.

cards.explanation: The slide’s nearby LDL annotation is too simple to establish one adipokine as the universal cause of elevated LDL.
cards.text: The adipokine schematic shows inflammatory signalling converging on {{c1::insulin resistance}}.
cards.question: The adipokine schematic shows inflammatory signalling converging on {{c1::insulin resistance}}.

cards.explanation: In this model, SOCS3 inhibits components of metabolic signalling. This is a particular cardiac/metabolic scheme, not every physiological IL-6 response.
cards.text: The displayed IL-6 pathway activates STAT3 and then {{c1::SOCS3}}.
cards.question: The displayed IL-6 pathway activates STAT3 and then {{c1::SOCS3}}.

cards.explanation: The schematic links inhibited signalling with lower GLUT4-related metabolic activity.
cards.text: Impaired insulin signalling can reduce insulin-stimulated {{c1::glucose uptake}}.
cards.question: Impaired insulin signalling can reduce insulin-stimulated {{c1::glucose uptake}}.

cards.explanation: It connects leptin with tumour/stromal pathways and invasion-related processes, not a deterministic claim that obesity or leptin inevitably produces metastasis.
cards.text: The adipose–tumour schematic highlights increased {{c1::leptin signalling}}.
cards.question: The adipose–tumour schematic highlights increased {{c1::leptin signalling}}.

cards.explanation: This is a histological/diagrammatic feature of inflamed adipose tissue, not a granuloma.
cards.text: Macrophages surrounding a dead adipocyte form a {{c1::crown-like structure}}.
cards.question: Macrophages surrounding a dead adipocyte form a {{c1::crown-like structure}}.

cards.explanation: This is one proposed pathway in obesity-related breast cancer biology, not a universal cause of every breast tumour.
cards.text: The diagram links adipose inflammation with increased aromatase and local {{c1::oestrogen production}}.
cards.question: The diagram links adipose inflammation with increased aromatase and local {{c1::oestrogen production}}.

cards.explanation: The illustration shows reciprocal communication, angiogenic effects and metabolic pathways rather than a single one-way causal chain.
cards.text: Adipocytes, macrophages and tumour cells can interact through {{c1::cytokine and adipokine signalling}}.
cards.question: Adipocytes, macrophages and tumour cells can interact through {{c1::cytokine and adipokine signalling}}.

slides.topic: Inflammation II — Chronic Inflammation & Disease — original page 64
slides.text:
◼Inflammatory response of prolonged duration in which active 
inflammation, tissue destruction and attempts at repair are 
occurring simultaneously.
▪Usually primary, but may follow recurrent acute 
   inflammation.
◼Its is characterized by:
▪infiltration of mononuclear cells. Lymphocytes, plasma 
cells and macrophages predominately.  
▪proliferation of fibroblasts and increases the risk of 
scaring (Repair with fibrosis and angiogenesis)
▪Tissue destruction by inflammatory cells
What is chronic inflammation?

slides.topic: Inflammation II — Chronic Inflammation & Disease — original page 65
slides.text:
• Persistent infection by certain microorganisms
– Ulcer
– tuberculosis
• Prolonged exposure to toxic agent
– Endogenous e.g. plasma lipids → atherosclerosis
– Pulmonary silicosis (silica in the lung)
• Autoimmunity
– Antibodies to self antigens → perpetual immune response.
– Rheumatoid arthritis
– Systemic lupus erythematosus 
– Multiple sclerosis
What causes chronic inflammation?

slides.topic: Inflammation II — Chronic Inflammation & Disease — original page 72
slides.text:
Non-specific chronic inflammation 
▪Has a diffuse accumulation of macrophages and 
lymphocytes at the site of injury. 
▪Persistent chemotaxis: 
- causes 
infiltration 
and 
accumulation 
of    
macrophages at  the inflamed area
- leads to fibroblast proliferation with subsequent 
scar formation
▪In many cases, the scar tissues replaces the 
normal connective and parenchymal tissues.
  e.g. tissue scar resulting from CI of the bowel causes narrowing of the 
bowel lumen.

slides.topic: Inflammation II — Chronic Inflammation & Disease — original page 73
slides.text:
Granulomatous inflammation 
▪It is a specific type of chronic inflammation. 
▪It is a protective response to chronic infection or foreign 
material, 
preventing 
dissemination 
and 
restricting 
inflammation.
▪A granuloma is a small lesion (1-2mm) and   typically is an 
aggregate of 5 or more epithelioid histiocytes (i.e. the 
modified macrophages that resemble epithelial cells).
▪ It is associated with agents which are poorly digested:
▪foreign bodies such as splinters, sutures, silica, and asbestos 
etc.,
▪drugs such as allopurinol and phenylbutazone in hepatic 
granulomas 
▪microorganisms that cause tuberculosis, syphilis, sarcoidosis, 
brucellosis, and deep fungal infections.

slides.text:
Local manifestations of inflammation
▪Local manifestations of inflammation are result of 
the vascular changes associated with acute 
inflammatory process (vasodialation and increased 
capillary permeability). The symptoms can be: 
redness, heat, swelling and pain.
  
▪Dependent upon its cause and the tissue involved.
▪  Range from swelling and the formation of 
   exudates to abscess formation and ulceration.

slides.topic: Inflammation II — Chronic Inflammation & Disease — original page 78
slides.text:
Systemic Manifestations of Inflammation
▪ The inflammatory response remains confined to a localized area 
under optimal conditions.
▪ In some cases, local injury can result in systemic manifestations 
as inflammatory mediators are released into the circulation.
▪  The most prominent systemic manifestations of inflammation 
are: 
-  changes in the levels of the plasma protein (i.e. acute  
   phase reactants).
-  haematological changes (increased levels of circulating  
leukocytes )
-  lymph node enlargement 
-  fever, weight loss, malaise, anorexia and nausea
-  sepsis and septic shock, which represent the sever 
   systemic manifestations of inflammation.

slides.topic: Inflammation II — Chronic Inflammation & Disease — original page 79
slides.text:
IL-1, IL-6 and TNFalpha (endogenous pyrogens) released  by 
macrophages act on the hypothalamus, muscle and fat cells to raise 
body temperature (fever)
How does fever helps the immune system fight infection?
1. Most bacterial and viral pathogens grow better at temperature lower 
than human body temperature (37C)
2. Human cells become more resistant to the deleterious effects of TNF 
alpha at raised temperatures
3. Adaptive immunity becomes more potent at higher temperatures 
(antigen processing is enhanced)
FEVER: a systemic effect of inflammation
Note: Bacterial products (called exogenous pyrogens) stimulate leukocytes to release 
cytokines…

slides.topic: Inflammation II — Chronic Inflammation & Disease — original page 86

Parallels between wound healing and tumorigenesis 
•
“Tumours are wounds that do not heal” 
 
 
Dvorak HF (1986) N Engl J Med 315:1650.
•
Tumours share many histological features with repairing tissues.
•
In both wound sites and tumours cell proliferation, survival and 
migration is accompanied by an inflammatory response (in response 
to GFs and cytokines).
•
During wound healing keratinocytes hyperproliferate, migrate and 
invade, similar to keratinocytes during malignant transformation in 
squamous cell carcinoma.
•
During repair in keratinocytes one third of the genes expressed are 
also present in squamous cell carcinoma. Pedersen et al. (2003) Oncogene 22: 3964
•
‘Wound’ signals in tumours can facilitate cancer progression.

Diet and chronic inflammation
Chronic inflammation is a metabolic inflammatory 
response:
The immune system responds to distress from adipocytes (fat 
cells) and other metabolic cell (liver, brain, muscle).
Visceral fat (fat around the internal organs) triggers 
inflammation:
Macrophages are activated to the site of the fat tissue and the 
body show a small but significant increase in markers of 
inflammation (i.e. Tumor necrosis factor-a (TNF-a), 
Interleukin-6 (-6) and c-reactive protein (CRP))
